options: A modern approach to data architecture and governance that emphasises decentralisation and domain-driven ownership of data products
A technique for combining data from several web sources into a single view
A centralised data warehouse managed by a monolithic data team
A disorganised datastore lacking master data, metadata and lineage
A single database that serves both transactional and analytical workloads
questions.explanation: Data Mesh is a modern approach to data architecture and governance that emphasises decentralisation and domain-driven ownership of data products. It is often confused with Data Mashup, but the two are totally different.

questions.stem: Which four key principles does Data Mesh revolve around?
options: Accuracy, Completeness, Consistency and Timeliness
Domain-Oriented Decentralisation, Data as a Product, Self-Service Data Infrastructure and Federated Governance
Extraction, Transformation, Loading and Visualisation
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability and Privacy
Hubs, Links, Satellites and Reference tables
questions.explanation: At its core, Data Mesh revolves around four principles: Domain-Oriented Decentralisation, Data as a Product (DAaP), Self-Service Data Infrastructure and Federated Governance.

questions.stem: In Data Mesh, what does a domain refer to?
options: A physical database server
A cloud region where data is stored
A specific business area or operational unit, such as marketing, sales or customer service
A single table in the data warehouse
A regulatory jurisdiction
questions.explanation: A domain, in the Data Mesh context, refers to a specific business area or operational unit, such as marketing, sales or customer service, and each domain is responsible for its own data products.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement that Data Mesh places on each data product?
options: Be discoverable and self-descriptive
Have clearly defined APIs for easy access
Include documentation, versioning and quality metrics
Be built and maintained by a central data engineering team
Be interoperable with other data products within and across domains
questions.explanation: Data products must be discoverable and self-descriptive, have clear APIs, include documentation, versioning and quality metrics, and be interoperable. Data Mesh moves ownership away from a central team to the domains.

questions.stem: What does Federated Governance provide in a Data Mesh?
options: Complete freedom for each domain with no organisation-wide policies
A single central team that approves every data product
Automatic deletion of short-lived datasets
A rule that each domain must use the same modelling technique
Consistency, compliance and quality across the ecosystem by setting global policies that domains implement in contextually appropriate ways
questions.explanation: Federated governance ensures consistency, compliance and quality across the organisation's data ecosystem, balancing autonomy and alignment by establishing global policies while allowing domains flexibility in how they implement them.

questions.stem: Regardless of the modelling technique used, what is described as the hallmark of a data product in a Data Mesh?
options: Interoperability
Normalisation to third normal form
Being stored in a single central warehouse
Being short-lived and purpose-specific
Being built with dimensional modelling
questions.explanation: Data products in a Data Mesh may use 3NF, dimensional or ensemble modelling, but their hallmark is interoperability: they must seamlessly exchange data within and across domains.

questions.stem: Which types of data asset are given as examples of what is NOT part of a Data Mesh?
options: Dimensional models and Data Vault models
Short-lived data sets and non-interoperable data assets
Data products owned by the marketing domain
Data products with versioning and quality metrics
Data pipelines and storage solutions
questions.explanation: Temporary data sets created for short-term analytical purposes, and data assets that cannot be shared or consumed by other domains or products, do not qualify as data products in a Data Mesh.

questions.stem: How many Data Meshes can an organisation have?
options: One per domain
One per data product
Only one per organisation
One per cloud provider
As many as there are business units
questions.explanation: Data Mesh is a conceptual model, and there can be only one Data Mesh per organisation. This prevents fragmentation and keeps all domains under a shared framework of principles and governance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a benefit of Data Mesh?
options: Scalability
Business alignment
Faster time to insight
Lower initial costs
Flexibility in technology choices
questions.explanation: The benefits listed are scalability, business alignment, faster time to insight, improved data quality and flexibility in technology choices. Initial costs are actually a challenge, since building self-service infrastructure and training teams needs upfront investment.

questions.stem: Which challenges are listed for implementing Data Mesh?
options: Data duplication, slow queries and vendor lock-in
Lack of SQL support, HDFS dependency and row storage
Missing master data, metadata and lineage
Fan traps, chasm traps and deep join chains
Cultural shift, skill development, complex governance and initial costs
questions.explanation: Implementing Data Mesh involves a cultural shift from centralised to decentralised, skill development within domains, complex federated governance, and initial costs for infrastructure and training.
